entities.name: The Japanese Classical Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Japanese Classical Corpus encompasses the foundational literary, historical, religious, and philosophical texts of Japanese civilization from the earliest written records (8th century CE) through the medieval period. Its pillars include: the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE) — the earliest mythological-historical chronicles establishing the Shinto cosmology and imperial genealogy; the Man'yoshu (c.

759 CE) — the oldest poetry anthology with 4,500+ poems in Old Japanese, reflecting all social classes from emperors to soldiers; the Tale of Genji (Genji Monogatari, c. 1000–1012 CE) by Lady Murasaki Shikibu — widely considered the world's first psychological novel and the supreme masterpiece of Japanese literature; the Pillow Book (c. 1002 CE) by Sei Shonagon — a brilliant miscellany of Heian court life; and the medieval Zen Buddhist and warrior literature including the Tale of the Heike (c.

1330), Bashō's haiku, Zeami's Noh drama treatises, and Dōgen's Shōbōgenzō. This corpus reveals a civilization of extraordinary aesthetic sensitivity, developing uniquely Japanese literary forms (mono no aware, wabi-sabi, mujo) that continue to influence world culture.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Japanese Classical Corpus played a pivotal role in shaping Japan's imperial genealogy and Shinto cosmology through its foundational texts like the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki. Its impact on Japanese literature, particularly with works like the Man'yoshu and Genji Monogatari, has had a lasting influence on Asian literary traditions.
